summary: This work measures microwave absorption from surface two-level systems in superconducting aluminum resonators and correlates losses with materials characterization, finding that the native 2.7 nm AlOx layer dominates losses with a loss tangent of $(1.74 ± 0.7) × 10^{-2}$, over three times higher than tantalum oxide. HF treatment reduces oxide thickness to 1.9 nm and lowers loss by a factor of 1.8, but rapid oxide regrowth and fabrication residues limit improvements, with Al interfaces estimated to contribute 27% of relaxation in state-of-the-art Ta-on-Si qubits incorporating Al Josephson junctions.
motivation: Recent millisecond-scale coherence demonstrations in tantalum-on-silicon transmons motivate detailed characterization of the aluminum oxide two-level system bath, since these qubits still use traditional Al/AlOx/Al Josephson junctions deposited in ultrahigh vacuum environments.
method: Power and temperature-dependent quality factor measurements on 40 CPW resonators with varied deposition conditions (200°C, 25°C, −72°C), fabrication methods (wet-etch, dry-etch, liftoff), and post-fabrication treatments (HF acid, H₂O₂) were correlated with X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, atomic force microscopy, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy to isolate TLS loss contributions from different interfaces.
result: Untreated Al resonators yield surface loss tangent $(3.19 ± 0.22) × 10^{-3}$; 49% HF treatment achieves $(1.77 ± 0.08) × 10^{-3}$ (40% reduction), approaching piranha-treated Ta performance of $(1.59 ± 0.07) × 10^{-3}$. Loss budgeting attributes 52.4% to AlOx, 27.7% to fabrication residues, and 19.8% to metal-substrate and substrate-air interfaces; the junction barrier oxide is inferred to be four orders of magnitude lower in loss tangent, suggesting rare strongly-coupled TLS occupancy in small-area junctions.
